title: Lutnick Faces Bipartisan Fire as Senators Vow Crackdown on AI Chip Leaks to China
excerpt: The Commerce Secretary has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10 as lawmakers question why Singapore-based Megaspeed was never blacklisted over alleged diversion of Nvidia chips.
body:
• Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces bipartisan Senate pressure over reports that advanced Nvidia AI chips reached Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm whose former executive Alice Huang is accused by US intelligence of contact with a Chinese spy agency.
  • Lutnick has agreed to testify voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10; Nvidia's Jensen Huang has been asked to appear on December 3, with subpoenas threatened if he declines.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly blamed Commerce for delay in restricting the sales; Republican Senator Thom Tillis says Lutnick should resign.
  • For readers: the fight is over how export controls are enforced — through the Commerce Department's Entity List and licensing — and new bipartisan chip export-control legislation is now promised in Congress.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing the sharpest bipartisan scrutiny of his tenure, as senators in both parties demand answers about how billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia AI chips were sold to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive is accused of being a Chinese spy — and why his department did not blacklist the firm.

The company at the centre of the row is Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. Its former executive Alice Huang is alleged, according to US intelligence officials, to have had contact with a Chinese intelligence service. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating in 2024 whether Nvidia chips supplied to Megaspeed were being diverted to China in violation of export restrictions; the investigation was later transferred to the Department of Justice, The New York Times reported. The Commerce Department has not placed Megaspeed on its Entity List, which restricts listed companies' access to American technology, and according to CBS News has not added any company to the list since October 2025.

"The idea that the Commerce Department has been allowing potentially not just some of these one-off descriptions of [chip sales] that Nvidia's been doing but through other Chinese shell companies — we deserve answers."

— Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), incoming chair, Senate Intelligence Committee

Pressure from both parties

Senator Mark Warner, the incoming chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said Lutnick has "a host of problems" and suggested the department may have allowed sensitive sales through companies beyond Megaspeed. Senator Tom Cotton, the committee's current chair, said he had warned the administration that advanced chips were getting past export controls: "Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other," he posted on X, as reported by The Hill.

The criticism is not only congressional. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick earlier this month over the failure to blacklist Megaspeed, according to The New York Times, and told CNBC he was frustrated by the delay: President Trump "made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s," Bessent said, adding that Commerce "has the pen." Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican on the Banking Committee, went further and said Lutnick should resign. Democrats, meanwhile, are pressing questions about possible financial conflicts of interest, including data centres in Southeast Asia that supplied computing power to China and any ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick once led and which is now run by his sons. The Commerce Department has said Lutnick has complied with all ethics rules.

In a letter to Lutnick, Senator Maria Cantwell, the incoming chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, wrote that the department "has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," and urged him to use the department's authority under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018.

What happens next

Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has asked Lutnick to testify on December 10 and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on December 3. Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily — "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," his spokesperson told CNN. Scott has warned that if Huang does not appear voluntarily, the committee is prepared to use subpoenas. The hearings will test both the enforcement of existing export controls and Congress's appetite for the tighter legislation Cotton has promised.
